Learning Objectives
Discuss the mechanism of metatarsal and phalangeal fractures.
Review indications for surgical and nonsurgical management of metatarsal and phalangeal
fractures.
Explain injuries associated with metatarsal and phalangeal fractures.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview

Fractures of the metatarsals and phalanges are common injuries that may result from low-
energy (most common) or high-energy trauma.
Metatarsal fractures may be divided by region: proximal metaphysis, diaphysis, head, and neck
Metatarsal fractures also may be grouped based on function of the bone: first metatarsal,
central metatarsals (second through fourth), and fifth metatarsal
Epidemiology
Metatarsal fractures account for as many as 35% of all foot fractures.
Metatarsal fractures may occur in isolation or in combination with other lower extremity
injuries. They may result from direct or indirect trauma and may result from low-energy
trauma or of high-energy trauma, such as crush injuries.
Metatarsal fractures are the most common fractures sustained during motorcycle trauma.
Metatarsal fractures are most common in individuals in their teenage years to forties.
Third metatarsal fractures are associated with adjacent fractures to the second or fourth
metatarsal in 63% of patients.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The forefoot extends from the tarsometatarsal joint to the tips of the toes.
The first metatarsal is the strongest metatarsal and bears approximately 40% of the weight of
the foot through the sesamoids, which lie under the first metatarsal head.
The second metatarsal may be the longest metatarsal. A long second metatarsal may increase
bending forces on this bone and, because of the tight ligamentous attachments and dense
pack geometry at the base of the second metatarsal, may result in stress fractures at the
proximal metaphysis or in the shaft.
The second metatarsal base is recessed in relation to the first and third metatarsals, creating
the keystone of the arch of the foot.
Vascular Anatomy
The fifth metatarsal vascular supply contains a watershed area at the proximal metaphyseal-
diaphyseal junction, which may contribute to poor healing in this region.

The plantar arch is an anastomosis of the lateral plantar artery (branch of the posterior tibial
artery) and the dorsalis pedis artery. It provides blood to the plantar foot and toes.
Muscles/Tendons
Flexor hallucis longus: inserts on the plantar aspect of the base of the distal phalanx of the big
toe
Peroneus longus: inserts on the lateral aspect of the first metatarsal base (also inserts on the
plantar aspect of the medial cuneiform); everts the foot and plantarflexes the ankle
Peroneus brevis: inserts on the base of the fifth metatarsal; everts the foot and plantarflexes
the ankle.
Peroneus tertius: inserts on the dorsal aspect of the base of the fifth metatarsal
Tibialis anterior: inserts on the base of the first metatarsal (also on the medial and plantar
aspects of the first cuneiform)
Joints and Ligaments
No direct proximal ligamentous connection is present between the first and second
metatarsals.
The medial (first tarsometatarsal joint) and middle (second and third tarsometatarsal joints)
columns have limited mobility in the sagittal plane compared with the lateral column (fourth
and fifth tarsometatarsal joints).
The central metatarsal bases (second through fourth) contain intermetatarsal (dorsal, central,
and plantar) ligamentous structures that link one to another for stability.
Distally, these central metatarsals contain a thick transverse ligament that connects them
indirectly through the plantar plates.
Lack of connection is present between the first and second metatarsals by these ligaments
because the Lisfranc ligament provides stability through its connection between the second
metatarsal and the medial cuneiform (Figure 1).
Distal intermetatarsal ligaments stabilize the second through fifth metatarsals

Musculature
The central metatarsals are the origin of the dorsal and plantar interosseous muscles, which
help provide stabilization for the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints. These muscles act as
deforming forces with metatarsal fractures.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Mechanisms of injury include a direct blow, avulsion, twisting, or inversion.
Stress fractures can occur and generally are associated with an acute increase in activity or
overuse. They frequently are associated with endocrine or metabolic disorders.
The first metatarsal bone bears 40% of the weight of the foot (one-half on each sesamoid
bone) during the midstance phase of gait.
Fractures of the first metatarsal may result from a direct blow or crush injury or from indirect
trauma, such as twisting injuries.
Fractures of the metatarsal neck and head (second to fourth metatarsal bones)

4/19

Many fractures of the metatarsal neck can be managed nonsurgically. Fractures of the
metatarsal neck in which severe angulation and plantar angulation are present may require
reduction and fixation. Fractures in which dorsal angulation or translation is present may
require reduction with fixation to prevent transfer metatarsalgia.
Fractures of the metatarsal head are rare and generally can be managed nonsurgically;
however, displaced, or intra-articular fractures may require closed or open reduction and
fixation.
Stress fractures may occur in any metatarsal; however, most occur in the neck of the second
metatarsal and commonly are observed in athletes or military recruits. These injuries are
managed nonsurgically, with post-management avoidance of impact exercises. Stress
fractures of the proximal metatarsals may be observed in dancers, runners, and basketball
players.
Multiple displaced fractures of the metatarsals with shortening of more than 3 or 4 mm may
result in loss of the normal cascade of the metatarsal heads and pain. These fractures
usually require surgical restoration of metatarsal length and internal fixation.
Central metatarsal fractures that are malaligned in varus or valgus but are well aligned in the
sagittal plane and maintain length often do not require open reduction and internal fixation
(ORIF).
Phalangeal fractures
Mechanism of fracture is a direct blow, crush injury, or axial loading.
Painful subungual hematoma may be associated with distal phalangeal fracture and usually
is managed nonsurgically; if observed early postinjury, the hematoma can be evacuated via a
hole in the nail.
Nonsurgical management consisting of closed reduction and buddy taping for 4 weeks
generally is indicated for injuries of the lesser toes.
In the hallux, surgical management is indicated for displaced articular injuries or angulated
proximal phalangeal fractures if closed reduction and percutaneous pinning fail. Failed closed
reduction can be converted to ORIF.
Injuries to the sesamoid bone
Injuries may result from direct impact with compression via hyperdorsiflexion with a
transverse fracture or via repetitive trauma.
Plain radiographs should include a sesamoid view to evaluate the articulation of the
sesamoid bone with the plantar aspect of the metatarsal head. MRI is useful in determining
the presence of a stress reaction or stress fracture.

5/19

Acute fractures or stress fractures of the sesamoid bones may be managed via padding and
immobilization in a hard-soled rocker-bottom shoe or controlled ankle motion boot for 4 to 8
weeks.
Excision of the sesamoid is performed in patients with a chronic symptomatic nonunion. The
potential complication of medial sesamoidectomy is hallux valgus, whereas lateral
sesamoidectomy may result in varus deformity of the hallux. Excision of both sesamoids may
result in a cock-up deformity of the hallux because of loss of the plantar plate and the flexor
hallucis brevis attachments.
Sesamoid ORIF with bone grafting is controversial with mixed results.
Risk Factors
Cavovarus alignment may predispose individuals to fractures of the fifth metatarsal because of
overload of the lateral column.
A long second metatarsal or hypermobile medial column may predispose individuals to stress
fractures of the second metatarsal.
Associated Injuries
In patients with a high-energy mechanism of injury or a crush injury, a high index of suspicion
should be maintained for Lisfranc injuries or compartment syndrome.
Injury Classification
Fractures of the fifth metatarsal
Type I fractures
Avulsion of the long plantar ligament, the lateral band of the plantar fascia, or contraction
of the peroneus brevis may result in type I fractures of the fifth metatarsal.
Management consists of weight bearing as tolerated in a stiff-soled shoe or controlled
ankle motion boot.
Surgical management may be necessary, although rarely, for fractures with large displaced
intra-articular fragments. Surgical treatment usually is necessary only in patients who
remain symptomatic after 8 to 12 weeks of nonsurgical treatment. Most patients who
undergo nonsurgical treatment go on to heal with no sequalae.

AAOS | Forefoot Trauma: Metatarsal and Phalangeal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004059
6/19

Nonunion is uncommon but can be managed via excision and repair of the peroneus brevis
tendon, as necessary.
Type II fractures
The metadiaphyseal region of the fifth metatarsal is an area of circulatory watershed,
resulting in a limited blood supply to this region. Fractures at the metadiaphyseal junction,
approximately 1.5 to 2.5 cm distal to the base of the fifth metatarsal, are commonly called
Jones fractures.
Because of the compromised blood supply in the metadiaphyseal region of the fifth
metatarsal, fractures in this region are at risk for nonunion. Therefore, patients with such
fractures should not bear weight for 6 to 8 weeks.
Acute ORIF with the use of screws, in combination with prolonged restriction of activity,
often is performed in athletes or active patients to minimize the risk for nonunion of a type
II fracture.
Type III fractures
Type III fractures are stress fractures of the diaphysis of the fifth metatarsal. Cavovarus
deformities create a rigid, plantarflexed, medial column of the foot, increasing stress in the
lateral column of the foot and predisposing individuals to such fractures.
Hereditary sensorimotor neuropathy and diabetic neuropathy may predispose individuals
to type III fractures by causing inability to sense overloading of the fifth metatarsal bone.
Nonsurgical management, consisting of non–weight bearing, is used for proximal fractures
in the vascular watershed area of the fourth and fifth metatarsals.
Screw fixation is indicated for the repair of type III fractures in patients with established
sclerosis and nonunion and in athletes, in whom a more rapid return to play is desired.
Bone grafting and/or structural foot realignment may be necessary to achieve the healing
of type III fractures and prevent recurrence, particularly in patients with an atrophic
nonunion.
Mechanics of Fractures
Fractures of the metatarsals may result from direct trauma, such as a crush injury, or from
indirect trauma, such as twisting mechanisms in sports activity.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History

A thorough patient history should be obtained in all patients with foot trauma.
This should include the mechanism of injury and any concomitant injuries.
Physical Examination
A standard physical examination should be performed in all patients.
In patients who sustained high-energy trauma, a thorough survey of the entire body should be
performed.
In patients with a crush injury and high-energy trauma, severe swelling of the foot may be an
indication of compartment syndrome.
A complete neurovascular examination should be performed. In patients in whom severe
swelling prevents the palpation of pulses, doppler evaluation may be performed to confirm
dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arterial flow.
A neurologic examination should be performed to confirm intact light touch sensation.
The skin should be evaluated for threatened areas, particularly in patients who sustained high-
energy trauma and in patients with a severely displaced fracture in whom the skin may be
tented.
Neurovascular Examination
A careful neurovascular examination, focusing on sensation and perfusion of the toes, should
be performed for all patients.
In patients who sustain high-energy trauma, paresthesia or decreased capillary refill to the
toes may be signs of compartment syndrome of the foot.
Substantially displaced fifth metatarsal base fractures may cause irritation of the sural nerve.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographic evaluation of metatarsal or phalangeal fractures should include AP, lateral, and
oblique views.
If possible, standing radiographs may help elucidate injuries to the Lisfranc complex.
Hindfoot alignment on standing radiographs may be important in evaluating fifth metatarsal
fractures in patients with a cavovarus foot.

9/3/26, 4:11 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004059
8/19

Computed Tomography
Should be used to evaluate intra-articular fractures of the proximal metatarsals
May be used to evaluate nonhealing stress fractures for sclerosis about the fracture
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is very sensitive in the diagnosis of metatarsal stress fractures if radiographs are
inconclusive.
MRI should be performed sparingly and only after repeated plain radiographs obtained 4 to 6
weeks postinjury fail to show callous if the diagnosis is unclear.
Bone Scintigraphy
Nuclear medicine imaging (technetium-99m bone scintigraphy) may be used to diagnose
stress fractures of the metatarsal. It should be used sparingly and only after repeated plain
radiographs obtained 4 to 6 weeks postinjury fail to show callous if the diagnosis is unclear.
Assessment of ankle dorsiflexion with the knee flexed and extended is part of any proper foot
examination. Gastrocnemius equinus often is a substantial cause of metatarsal overload and
stress fracture.
Differential Diagnosis
Often, a metatarsal may have cortical thickening best observed on a weight-bearing oblique
view. This is especially common in patients with progressive collapsing foot deformity or pes
plano adductovalgus, in which the lesser metatarsals are overloaded.
Cortical hypertrophy without frank stress fracture may result in pain similar to that of stress
fractures.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Isolated lesser metatarsal neck fracture with minimal angulation

AAOS | Forefoot Trauma: Metatarsal and Phalangeal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004059
9/19

Isolated lesser metatarsal (second to fourth) shaft fracture with less than 2 to 3 mm of
shortening and without severe angulation that affects the cascade of the metatarsal heads.
Distal fifth metatarsal oblique fractures, even if displaced, typically can be managed
nonsurgically.
Multiple metatarsal shaft fractures with displacement in the sagittal plane. Displacement in the
AP plane is not as critical if the metatarsal heads are properly aligned for weight bearing.
Contraindications
Fractures with substantial displacement that tent or threaten the skin or the neurovascular
structures
Fractures of the first metatarsal base that lead to joint instability at the first tarsometatarsal
joint
Multiple metatarsal neck fractures with loss of the normal cascade
Substantially displaced or shortened isolated metatarsal shaft fractures that alter the weight-
bearing cascade of the forefoot
Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical Fracture Management
Closed reduction of displaced metatarsal neck fractures may be attempted; however, if
multiple metatarsal neck fractures are present, instability may lead to inability to maintain
alignment.
Isolated lesser metatarsal neck fractures may be managed with the use of a fracture shoe or
fixed ankle walker boot with heel–weight bearing. Healing typically takes approximately 6 to 12
weeks.
Multiple nondisplaced metatarsal shaft fractures may require cast immobilization or a fixed
ankle walker boot and a period of non–weight bearing.
Stress fractures of the second to fourth metatarsals may be managed with the use of a fixed
ankle walker boot until radiographic healing is observed and pain resolves.
Fifth metatarsal base (type I) or distal fifth metatarsal shaft fractures may be managed with the
use of a fracture shoe or a fixed ankle walker boot with weight bearing as tolerated.
Type II fifth metatarsal fractures (Jones fractures), if managed nonsurgically, should be
managed via cast immobilization/a controlled ankle motion boot and non–weight bearing for 6
to 8 weeks because they are associated with a high rate of delayed union or nonunion.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:11 PM

Outcomes
Outcomes of metatarsal fractures managed nonsurgically are satisfactory if the weight-bearing
cascade of the forefoot is maintained.
If substantial malunion with shortening or sagittal deformity occurs, the weight-bearing
cascade of the forefoot may be altered, leading to transfer metatarsalgia to adjacent
metatarsal heads, at which loads will increase.
Surgical Management
Indications
First metatarsal
Fractures of the first metatarsal are acted on by strong tendon forces that tend to displace
the fractures into dorsiflexion with displacement of the Meary line and weight-bearing
alignment. Therefore, complete fractures of the first metatarsal should be followed closely,
with early management via ORIF if displacement occurs.
For fractures of the first metatarsal, clinically meaningful displacement, intra-articular
fracture, or displacement of the Meary talar–first metatarsal line (usually into dorsiflexion),
surgical management may be required.
Proximal fractures may be associated with Lisfranc injuries and require surgical
management.
Surgical management should be considered for fractures with sagittal plane angulation
because they may alter the weight-bearing mechanics of the entire forefoot.
Contraindications
Peripheral artery disease
Smoking (relative contraindication)
In patients with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus, extra caution is required, with vigilance for
signs of Charcot arthropathy. If fixation is performed, more robust constructs should be used
via techniques such as dual plating. In addition, any gaps should be bone grafted (Figure 2).

Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
In most patients, standard radiographs are sufficient for planning surgical management of
metatarsal fractures.
CT scans may aid in evaluation of intra-articular fractures and comminuted fractures.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:11 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004059
12/19

In patients with a stress fracture or nonunion, metabolic workup, including evaluation and
management of vitamin D deficiency, should be considered.
Swelling should be evaluated preoperatively. In patients with severe soft-tissue swelling,
surgical treatment should be delayed. The patient should undergo splint immobilization with
the ankle and subtalar joints in neutral and the leg elevated to waist level. Overelevation has
been reported to result in peripheral circulation deficits.
Patient Positioning
Metatarsal fractures generally are fixed with the patient in the supine position.
For fifth metatarsal fracture fixation, the placement of a bump or bean bag under the
ipsilateral buttock is helpful to internally rotate the leg, which improves access to the lateral
midfoot/forefoot.
Alternatively, the patient is placed in the lateral position and the foot is brought posteriorly off
the bed and placed on the stage of the fluoroscope. This facilitates ORIF of the fifth metatarsal.
Surgical Approaches
First metatarsal fractures may be approached via a dorsal or medial incision. The dorsomedial
cutaneous nerve should be identified and protected.
The second through fourth metatarsals are approached via a dorsal incision. Depending on
the number of metatarsal fractures being manage, this may be done via a single incision
centered over a metatarsal, an incision placed between two adjacent metatarsals, or via
multiple incisions. The branches of the superficial peroneal nerve should be protected, as
should the deep peroneal nerve and the dorsalis pedis artery, which run with the extensor
hallucis brevis between the first and second metatarsals.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
Options for fracture fixation include Kirschner wires, screws, or plates. Fusion of the first
tarsometatarsal joint may be necessary for comminuted fractures or patients with a late
diagnosis.
Plate osteosynthesis should be considered for displaced metatarsal shaft fractures and
multiple metatarsal shaft fractures (Figure 3).

Postoperative Management
Patients undergoing metatarsal fracture fixation typically undergo splint immobilization to
allow for wound healing and edema management.
After 2 weeks, patients may be transitioned to a removable fixed ankle boot or postoperative
shoe, depending on the location and severity of the injury.
For distal fractures, early, protected heel–weight bearing may be initiated after 2 weeks
postoperatively; however, for more comminuted or proximal injuries, weight bearing may be
delayed as long as 6 weeks postoperatively or until healing is confirmed radiographically.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
A radiographic series of the uninjured foot is helpful during ORIF because it serves as a
template for the surgeon.

In petite patients, the lesser metatarsal shafts may be very small.
Distal metatarsal shaft or neck fractures may have minimal bone stock for fixation distal to the
fracture.
In fixing fifth metatarsal fractures, attention should be given to the natural bow of the fifth
metatarsal, especially for intramedullary screw placement. The starting point for such screws
should be high and inside, meaning dorsal and medial at the proximal fifth metatarsal to avoid
distal cortical disruption or distraction of the fracture site.
In managing multiple comminuted lesser metatarsal fractures, beginning with the most length
stable fracture often is helpful to aid in attaining appropriate length of the other metatarsals.
Complications
Nonunion
Nonunion is relatively uncommon for fractures of the first through third metatarsals.
Proximal fourth metatarsal fracture nonunions have been described and may be similar to
Jones fractures of the fifth metatarsal.
Type II and type III fifth metatarsal fractures may progress to nonunion at a higher rate than
other metatarsals (Figure 4).

Malunion
Malunion may result in dysfunction with plantar flexion of the foot and shortening.
Dorsiflexion malunion results in transfer metatarsalgia to the adjacent metatarsals.
Pain
Complex regional pain syndrome may occur, especially after high-energy trauma or crush
injuries.
Intra-articular fractures may lead to degenerative joint disease and require additional
management.
Infection
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:11 PM
AAOS | Forefoot Trauma: Metatarsal and Phalangeal Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004059
16/19

Postoperative infection and wound complications may be minimized by allowing soft-tissue
inflammation to resolve before surgical management and by minimizing additional soft-tissue
trauma during surgical management.
Pinning for lesser metatarsal neck fractures may lead to intra-articular infection/a septic MTP
joint.
Malalignment
Malalignment or malunion may lead to altered weight-bearing mechanics of the forefoot,
transfer metatarsalgia, and plantar hyperkeratosis.
Hardware Failure
Similar to any fracture, nonunion or delayed union may lead to hardware failure.
Distal metatarsal fractures with limited bone stock distally may provide poor fixation and lead
to failure of fixation.
Hardware Malpositioning
In performing intramedullary fixation of fifth metatarsal fractures, a poor entry point or the
use of a screw that is too long may lead to cortical disruption distally or distraction of the
fracture site.
In fixing distal lesser metatarsal fractures with the use of plate and screw constructs, distal
hardware placement may interfere with normal MTP joint motion.
Stiffness
Stiffness may occur in the MTP joints after metatarsal fracture, and with solid fixation, early
motion should be initiated.
After ORIF, adhesions may form at the toe extensor tendons, limiting motion of the toes and
the MTP joints.
Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
Patients should be screened for risk factors for deep vein thrombosis, including personal or
family history of deep vein thrombosis and medications that may lead to a hypercoagulable

17/19

state, such as birth control medication.
No consensus guidelines for chemoprophylaxis for metatarsal fractures exist in the United
States. In other areas of the world, prophylaxis is the standard of care.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
In placing hardware along the lateral fifth metatarsal, the sural nerve is at risk.
Care must be taken in approaching metatarsals dorsally to protect the branches of the
superficial peroneal nerve and the deep peroneal nerve.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Patients with metatarsal fractures may have associated foot deformity, such as cavovarus.
Often, gastrocnemius equinus is present, which can be appreciated by examining the
contralateral uninjured foot and ankle. If equinus is present, then part of any surgical
procedure should include gastrocnemius release. Failure to appreciate equinus and perform
gastrocnemius release may lead to failed surgical management.
